item.title: A $\theta$-implicit hybrid particle-in-cell algorithm for kinetic simulations of magnetized plasmas
item.description: arXiv:2611.00127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid particle-in-cell (PIC) models with kinetic ions and an inertialess electron fluid are widely used to simulate magnetized plasmas at ion scales, but explicit time advances are constrained by the whistler-wave CFL condition $\dt \propto \Delta x^2$, and the sub-cycling and artificial dissipation used to mitigate it carry accumulating costs. We present a $\theta$-implicit hybrid PIC algorithm, implemented in the open-source GPU-capable code WarpX, in which fields and particles are advanced as a single nonlinear system solved by a particle-suppressed Jacobian-free Newton--Krylov method: the particles are nonlinearly eliminated, the electric field of the generalized Ohm's law is the sole unknown, and mass matrices remove all particle operations from the linear iterations. The electron pressure is advanced inside the nonlinear solve, and the scheme satisfies a discrete energy law whose single dissipation term vanishes at $\theta = 1/2$ and damps only temporally under-resolved modes for $\theta > 1/2$. The advance reproduces parallel and perpendicular wave dispersion including the ion Bernstein modes, conserves total energy to machine roundoff where the explicit advance heats secularly, does not develop the cold-beam finite-grid instability, and reproduces the $m=0$ instability of a Bennett pinch in RZ geometry. We conclude with 3D simulations of a field-reversed configuration initialized from a Grad--Shafranov equilibrium, comparing the explicit and implicit advances on the growth of the tilt instability and the preservation of trapped magnetic flux.
item.dc:creator: Prabhat Kumar, William J. White, Stephen E. Clark

item.title: Transient subtraction method: An alternative approach for variance reduction in dissipative particle dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.00330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The efficient and accurate computation of transport coefficients remains a numerical challenge in dissipative particle dynamics (DPD), which can require substantial sampling to control statistical uncertainty. We extend recent results obtained in Langevin dynamics to consider the transient subtraction method for reducing the variance of transport coefficient estimations in DPD. The system is initialised by perturbing equilibrium samples, and its relaxation towards equilibrium is monitored under the reference dynamics. A reference trajectory, initialised at equilibrium and driven by the same Brownian noise, provides a control variate for the transient response. We apply the transient subtraction method to the computation of the mobility and the shear viscosity in a Lennard-Jones fluid in DPD. The shear viscosity is obtained from the time-integrated response of a Fourier observable associated with the longitudinal velocity. Numerical comparisons with the naive transient estimator show that the transient subtraction method reduces the variance at various integration times, and the reduction is more pronounced with a higher friction coefficient. These results indicate that the transient subtraction method is able to improve the statistical precision of transport coefficient estimations in DPD and reduce the number of trajectories needed to attain a prescribed standard error.
item.dc:creator: Xinyi Wu, Xiaocheng Shang

item.title: ROSE: Deep Learning exchange-correlation functional from reduced density-matrix representations
item.description: arXiv:2611.00826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce ROSE, a deep-learning exchange--correlation energy functional built from the occupied-state density matrix. On GMTKN55 and on additional external benchmarks considered in this work, ROSE improves over modern neural network functionals trained under matched protocols and is on average more accurate than, or on par with, most hybrid and range-separated hybrid functionals considered here. On the experimental benchmarks considered here it has leading accuracy across hybrids, range separated hybrids, and neural functionals. These results motivate nonlocal density-matrix representations as a route to systematic improvement of learned XC functionals with low computational cost.
item.dc:creator: Kirill Kulaev, Alexander Ryabov, Bogdan Protsenko, Alexander Guda, Alexander Soldatov, Evgeny Burnaev, Vladimir Vanovskiy

item.title: Structure-Preserving Full Approximation Scheme for Real-Space Hartree-Fock Equations
item.description: arXiv:2611.00880v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a structure-preserving full approximation scheme (FAS) for the real-space restricted Hartree-Fock equations. The method treats the orbital equations, Coulomb and exchange pair potentials, and orthonormality constraints as a coupled nonlinear system on a hierarchy of finite-element spaces. Forced Gram targets, occupied-frame alignment, and auxiliary-variable reconstruction provide constraint compatibility and occupied-rotation equivariance under suitable assumptions. Analysis of the full self-consistent response identifies an elliptic kinetic principal part, motivating the multilevel treatment. The resulting solver, FAS-H, combines FAS cycles with a residual-triggered horizontal Newton correction on the finest grid. Numerical experiments on eight closed-shell systems show convergence in 4-11 cycles across three grid levels. Across 24 system-grid comparisons, FAS-H is 1.60-5.02 times faster than SCF and uses 68-91% less weighted FFT work, while standalone horizontal Newton is faster in some cases.
item.dc:creator: Yuejia Zhang

item.title: Quantum HHL Algorithm for Solving 1D Linear Advection Equation Using Explicit and Implicit Finite Difference Schemes
item.description: arXiv:2611.01167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study develops and implements a Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd (HHL) quantum algorithm for solving a one-dimensional linear advection equation with periodic boundary conditions. The governing equation is first discretized using a classical finite difference (FD) scheme to obtain a linear system suitable for quantum solution. We present a newly designed, circuit-level implementation of HHL assembled from Qiskit circuit components and exploit the circulant structure of the periodic discretization matrices through Fourier-based matrix evolution. The HHL algorithm is benchmarked with three explicit schemes and one implicit scheme. The implicit scheme requires a nontrivial linear solve arising from the discretized PDE on progressively finer grids, whereas the explicit schemes provide different input fields for testing state preparation and reconstruction with identity coefficient matrices. HHL solution states are validated against direct classical solves in noiseless simulation. For hardware execution, the periodic matrix structure permits a Fourier implementation that applies reciprocal eigenvalues without phase estimation. Results on the IBM Rensselaer Nighthawk processor are compared at a shared final time. Noiseless reconstructed fields approach the transported profile on resolved grids, while substantial hardware errors remain for both explicit and implicit schemes. Crank-Nicolson remains exceptionally well-conditioned and utilizes similar circuit re sources to the explicit controls, proving that hardware degradation in our tests was not driven by poor matrix conditioning. Ultimately, this study shows new means for HHL algorithms to study quantum CFD problems involving advection equations with implicit time integrations, while demonstrating how state preparation and measurement affect the practical performance of quantum solvers on current devices.
item.dc:creator: Batuhan Yalcin, Lucy T. Zhang

item.title: Variational learning of energy-stable macroscopic flow equations from microscopic laws
item.description: arXiv:2611.01432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a generalized variational approach for constructing energy-stable macroscopic partial differential equations (PDEs) directly from microscopic physical laws. Rather than fitting the PDE evolution for prescribed variables from macroscopic trajectories, we construct an extendable variational structure by adjoining auxiliary variables to seek autonomous reduced dynamics in an enlarged state space. By defining these variables as micro--macro encoders with explicit microscopic counterparts, we cast the learning problem as the sample-wise joint identification of the reduced state representation and the variational ingredients from time-discrete data, enabling systematic law-level transfer across scales. The resulting PDEs preserve frame indifference, physical constraints, and energy stability by construction, and admit a fluctuation--dissipation-consistent stochastic extension. Numerical results for the non-Newtonian hydrodynamics of polymeric fluids show that the learned models capture the viscoelastic responses induced by nonlinear and heterogeneous molecular interactions beyond empirical closures.
item.dc:creator: Pei Ge, Huan Lei

item.title: Quantum simulation of dissipative acoustic and elastic waves by Schr\"odingerisation: absorbing boundaries and explicit polynomial-size circuits
item.description: arXiv:2611.02357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Explicit quantum circuits for the acoustic and elastic wave equations, obtained by Hamiltonian simulation of their first-order forms, conserve energy and therefore describe closed domains: an outgoing wave reflects off the edge of the computational region or, with periodic boundaries, wraps around and re-enters from the opposite side. We open the domain with the simplest physical absorber, a graded sponge layer in which every wave field is damped at a rate that grows towards the outer edge, and implement the resulting dissipative dynamics on a quantum simulator by Schr\"odingerisation, which turns a non-unitary linear evolution into a family of unitary ones by means of a single auxiliary variable. We derive the whole chain from the partial differential equation to the circuit, in one, two and three dimensions. An independent finite-difference solver confirms that damping all wave fields absorbs far better than the common velocity-only damping mask. For the sponge the quantum analysis is sharp: recovery is exact on the whole non- negative half of the auxiliary axis at every time; that axis can be truncated periodically at a length set by the largest damping rate and the simulated time; and the success probability is a fixed constant, about 0.4, times the fraction of the energy not yet absorbed, with only one or two auxiliary qubits measured. On the circuit side, the damping step, which generic synthesis compiles into a number of controlled-NOT gates exponential in the number of qubits, factorises exactly into polynomially many multi-controlled phase gates. Gate-level simulations on up to 25 qubits agree with the classical solutions of the damped wave equations.
item.dc:creator: Hoang Anh Nguyen, Ali Tura

item.title: Maximal correlation and optimal transformations of probability distributions in tensor-train format: a variational algorithm
item.description: arXiv:2611.02731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The correlation between two subsystems $A$ and $B$ of a many-body system is usually measured through a pair of observables chosen in advance. The Hirschfeld-Gebelein-R\'enyi maximal correlation removes the choice: it is the largest correlation coefficient between any function of the configuration of $A$ and any function of the configuration of $B$, and the two functions that reach it, the optimal transformations, are the observables that carry the correlation. Both follow from a singular value decomposition (SVD) of the joint distribution normalized by its marginals, a matrix whose dimension is the number of configurations. We show that this SVD can be computed variationally for a classical distribution of discrete variables, such as the Boltzmann distribution of a spin model, given in the tensor-train (matrix-product) format, without ever forming the matrix. The optimal transformations are sought as tensor trains; each step updates a single core in closed form, and the inverse of a small matrix contracted from the distribution and the remaining cores performs the division by the marginals core by core. Every iterate is a feasible pair, so the objective is a lower bound on the maximal correlation that increases monotonically, and the cost grows linearly with the number of variables. The algorithm reproduces the exact SVD on small systems, recovers the known nonlinear optimal transformations of synthetic distributions of up to ten angular variables ($10^{15}$ configurations), and, for the bipartite antiferromagnetic model with $2^{32}$ configurations, returns an optimal transformation that is a function of the group magnetization, linear above the transition and sign-like below it: the staggered order parameter is read off from the distribution instead of being postulated.
item.dc:creator: Kayo Kinjo, Jun Ohkubo

item.title: Site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer for symmetry-constrained crystal generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.02906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative models for crystal structure prediction (CSP) have expanded the search space for novel materials and improved screening efficiency. However, simultaneously generating stable and novel structures remains challenging because of the complex structural and physical constraints governing crystals. To address this challenge, we propose site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer model (ST2M), a symmetry-guided discrete--continuous diffusion framework incorporating degree-of-freedom masks and conditioned on Wyckoff patterns. ST2M represents crystal structures as sequences of independent occupied Wyckoff orbits and employs a twin-branch Transformer to jointly denoise discrete and continuous variables. In our experiments, ST2M achieves a structural validity of 96.37\%. For known patterns in dataset, 23.86\% of generated structures simultaneously satisfy stability, uniqueness, and novelty criteria, representing a relative improvement of 68.15\% over the best-performing baseline. First-principles calculations identify a total of 21 previously unreported stable structures among selected candidates with low predicted energies. These results demonstrate that ST2M can generate chemically viable crystal candidates under prescribed crystallographic constraints and generalize to unknown Wyckoff patterns, providing a practical route to accelerated materials discovery.
item.dc:creator: Junchi Liu, Haoran Si, Luo Yan, Sergei Tretiak, Liujiang Zhou

item.title: Noise-resilient collective order through temporal memory in self-propelled particles
item.description: arXiv:2611.03003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal memory can stabilise collective motion by filtering noisy local observations, but persistent information can also impede adaptation when the collective state changes. We investigate this competition in Vicsek-type systems using two distinct alignment rules: a finite buffer of past observations and a recursive update of an internal directional state. In both models, increasing effective memory shifts the loss of polar order to stronger noise and can restore ordered motion under conditions for which the corresponding memoryless Vicsek model is disordered. The stationary responses of the two models show an approximate correspondence when parameterised by a kernel-based effective memory, consistent with temporal averaging playing a common role in their ordering behaviour rather than from the details of the memory implementation. Their transient dynamics, however, are not determined by effective memory alone. Following a collective perturbation, recovery is fastest at an intermediate memory depth and becomes slower when outdated observations are retained too strongly. Temporal integration therefore produces a trade-off: deeper memory improves noise resilience, whereas excessive persistence reduces responsiveness. These results identify memory depth as a control parameter that separates the optimisation of stationary order from that of dynamical recovery in noisy active systems.
item.dc:creator: Mihir Durve, Sauro Succi, Antonio Celani

item.title: Fracture-Bench: A Controlled Benchmark Suite for Machine Learning Surrogates in Phase-Field Fracture Mechanics
item.description: arXiv:2611.03473v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly proposed to replace phase-field fracture simulations in many-query tasks such as uncertainty quantification, inverse analysis and design. Little controlled evidence shows which architectures are reliable, for which fracture problems and how far beyond their training data. We introduce Fracture-Bench, an open benchmark of two phase-field datasets with fixed splits, common test metrics and a description of each dataset's physical regime. Dataset~1 contains 1,000 AT2 simulations of multiple cracks growing from a notched hole in a hyperelastic plate under random non-uniform biaxial boundary displacements (44 load steps, $128\times128$ grid). Dataset~2 contains 4,000 PF-CZM simulations of a pre-cracked plate with two inclusions, each ten times stiffer or more compliant than the matrix ($128\times256$ grid). We train a Fourier neural operator (FNO), DeepONet, Latent DeepONet, a UNet and a conditional diffusion model on identical splits and compare one test metric per dataset, training time, inference time and model size. On Dataset~1, FNO and Latent DeepONet attain mean test errors of order $10^{-6}$, about ten times lower than UNet and DeepONet. On Dataset~2, the diffusion model is most accurate, with about one sixth of the UNet error, but requires \SI{706}{s} per prediction versus \SI{6}{ms} for UNet. For all architectures, most of the error occurs in the final load steps, after crack localization. Dataset~2 contains initial cracks less than one grid cell apart that produce qualitatively different paths. Architecture rankings therefore depend on the task, and errors averaged over densely sampled inputs reveal little about near-bifurcation cases. Data, codes, splits, regime descriptors and generalization splits are public, with a protocol for adding under-represented regimes such as mixed-mode, three-dimensional and experimentally paired fracture.
item.dc:creator: Meenu Krishnan U., Maryam Hakimzadeh, Indrashish Saha, Meer Mehran Rashid, Lori Graham-Brady, Somdatta Goswami

item.title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2611.03485v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The shear piezoelectric coefficient $e_{15}$ governs the shear-mode electromechanical coupling in piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) and surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices, but measuring it typically requires destructive resonance testing on dedicated specimens. On simulated data, $e_{15}$ can instead be recovered non-destructively from sparse, noisy subsurface wavefield observations using a constrained physics-informed neural network (PINN). By building exact spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers directly into the network output, the clamped, grounded boundaries and resting initial state hold automatically, leaving the loss with only the interior equations of coupled electro-elastodynamics and the data misfit. Non-dimensional scaling brings all governing coefficients within one decade of O(1), and the setup removes the boundary and initial-condition penalty weights that soft-constraint methods must tune. In a six-way comparison (plane-strain PZT-5H, manufactured wavefield, 30 dB noise), a soft-penalty baseline with adaptive weights converges to an erroneous $e_{15}$ in four of the five runs (51.7% mean error), and fixed penalties reach an error of 0.85% only after a second-order optimization stage. The constrained formulations reach mean $e_{15}$ errors between 0.15% and 0.51% with held-out displacement errors below 1%. Within these variants, the spatial multiplier gives rapid first-order convergence, and the quadratic temporal multiplier lowers the early-time electrostatic residual by a factor of 6.8 versus a linear one. On finite-element data along one subsurface line, the full formulation recovers $e_{15}$ with 1.19% mean error at 30 dB and keeps it between 0.65% and 2.71% across a 40 to 0 dB noise sweep. Finally, training on displacements alone still recovers $e_{15}$ with mean errors of 0.45% on finite-element and 1.64% on manufactured data.
item.dc:creator: Suhas Suresh Bharadwaj

item.title: A geometry-aware framework for electromagnetic fields in GATE 10
item.description: arXiv:2611.00376v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Objective. An increasing number of medical-physics applications require the modelling of charged-particle transport in electromagnetic (EM) fields. We aim to provide GATE 10 users with a flexible mechanism for defining such fields in Monte Carlo simulations while preserving the native Geant4 particle-transport machinery. Approach. Our framework separates the handling of coordinates from EM field evaluation. Fields are attached to geometry volumes, defined in their local frame, and represented by analytic expressions, field maps, or arbitrary Python functions. They automatically follow the position and orientation of these volumes, including in nested and dynamic geometries. We validated the framework against native Geant4 transport and tested coordinate transformations, nested volumes, and dynamic geometry. We also compared the computational cost of the three field representations. Main results. The framework reproduced the native Geant4 trajectories exactly for all tested field types with direct Geant4 counterparts. Coordinate transformations introduced only floating-point-level differences, while simulations with dynamically changing geometry reproduced the equivalent static configurations exactly. All three representations produced equivalent transport. Mapped fields added at most 18% to the single-threaded runtime of analytic fields, while Python functions required 6.9 times as much. The compiled representations scaled with the number of threads, whereas Python functions became slower as threads were added. Significance. The framework adds flexible, geometry-aware EM field definitions to GATE 10 without modifying the underlying Geant4 transport machinery, and is part of the open-source GATE 10 codebase. It also provides a basis for extending GATE 10 with additional field representations in the future.
item.dc:creator: Marc Ballestero Rib\'o (Center for Proton Therapy, Paul Scherrer Institute, Villigen, Switzerland, Department of Physics, ETH Z\"urich, Z\"urich, Switzerland), Carla Winterhalter (Center for Proton Therapy, Paul Scherrer Institute, Villigen, Switzerland), Antony John Lomax (Department of Physics, ETH Z\"urich, Z\"urich, Switzerland), Sairos Safai (Center for Proton Therapy, Paul Scherrer Institute, Villigen, Switzerland)

item.title: Efficient Interpolation of the Bethe-Salpeter Hamiltonian at Arbitrary Momenta
item.description: arXiv:2611.00928v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop an efficient reciprocal-space method to reconstruct the static Bethe-Salpeter (BSE) Hamiltonian at arbitrary crystal momenta from coarse first-principles grids. Bloch states are interpolated within an optimally smooth Wannier subspace, while the screened Coulomb interaction is reconstructed from the dielectric response. This decouples the electron-hole transition momenta and transferred momentum from the underlying ab initio sampling. We benchmark the method on monolayer hBN, monolayer MoS$_2$, and bulk GaAs against explicit ab initio calculations, finding excellent agreement for dense-grid Bloch states, dielectric screening, and BSE optical spectra. Furthermore, our cost analysis estimates speedups of up to $22\times$ on the grids considered here. Arbitrary transferred-momentum sampling gives direct access to the long-wavelength exciton dispersion: in hBN and MoS$_2$, we resolve the nonanalytic behaviour induced by long-range electron-hole exchange at momenta well below the spacing of practical uniform grids. For bulk GaAs, locally refined transition-momentum sampling yields a converged binding energy for the threefold-degenerate lowest exciton, in close agreement with experiment and reference calculations, using far fewer BSE points than conventional uniform meshes. As the present framework provides exciton energies and amplitudes at arbitrary crystal momenta, it opens the way to incorporating ab initio excitonic effects into nonlocal electron-phonon vertices and to extensions towards exciton-phonon interactions and nonequilibrium exciton dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Stefano Mocatti, Xiangzhou Zhu, Giulio Volpato, Pierluigi Cudazzo, Matteo Calandra, Giovanni Marini

item.title: Optimally Weighted Constrained Shadow Tomography for Reduced Density Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2611.01079v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate measurement of reduced density matrices (RDMs) is central to quantum simulations of many-fermion systems, but the required measurement resources remain a significant challenge. Constrained shadow tomography (CST) combines randomized measurements with $N$-representability conditions to reconstruct physically valid RDMs from limited measurement data. Here we improve CST by orthogonalizing the measurement constraints and using the resulting singular values to determine the relative weight of each independent measurement direction according to how strongly it is sampled by the quantum computer. These optimally weighted constraints are incorporated into the semidefinite program through a least-squares objective implemented with a Schur-complement relaxation. We demonstrate the approach for hydrogen chains on a quantum simulator and for azobenzene on a quantum processor. In both cases, optimally weighted CST systematically improves the accuracy of the reconstructed 2-RDM without increasing the measurement budget, providing a more measurement-efficient approach to partial tomography for quantum simulations of correlated fermions.
item.dc:creator: Yuchen Wang, Irma Avdic, Michael Rose, Lillian I. Payne, Noah Garrett, Madhubani Mukherjee, Leah P. Weisburn, Nate Earnest-Noble, Kevin J. Sung, David A. Mazziotti

item.title: Atomistic Insights into MOCVD Growth of GaAs using a Closed Loop Autonomous System Combining Directed Reinforcement Learning and Kinetic Monte Carlo Simulations
item.description: arXiv:2611.01646v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conventional process optimization of the Metal-Organic Chemical Vapor Deposition (MOCVD) growth parameters to achieve high-quality thin films relies on iterative, resource-intensive experimental runs. While predictive modeling can circumvent this cost and effort, simulating thin-film growth is constrained by the vastly different length and time scales of the deposition process. While continuum (e.g., Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD)) and first-principles methods (e.g., Molecular Dynamics (MD)) struggle to balance experimental length/time scales and atomistic accuracy, Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) bridges this divide by resolving atomistic events whilst remaining tractable at experimental length and time scales. However, the accuracy of KMC relies on kinetic rate parameters that require costly density functional theory (DFT) calculations. In order to circumvent this, we present a framework that calibrates the rate parameters directly against experimental growth data. A forward KMC growth model is coupled in a closed loop with a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) optimizer that navigates the high-dimensional parameter space, with the search steered by the degree of rate control of each reaction rate parameter. The approach invokes no material-specific assumptions and hence, any deposition process whose forward kinetics can be reduced to a set of rate-controlled events is amenable to the same treatment. We demonstrate it for the MOCVD of GaAs, where the calibrated model captures the characteristic temperature dependence of the measured growth rate. The framework is also able to recover the three well known kinetic regimes characterized by change in the rate determining step from precursor chemisorption to desorption. As a result, the framework converts routinely measured growth data into a mechanistically interpretable model of the deposition process.
item.dc:creator: Hrishi V. Harsora, Ashutosh Krishna Amaram, Raghavan Ranganathan, Tarun K. Agarwal

item.title: Pore-scale mechanisms of capillary imbibition in cement-based materials revealed by direct numerical simulations in a realistic FIB-SEM microstructure
item.description: arXiv:2611.01901v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Moisture transport in cement-based materials involves transient multiphase flow through highly irregular pore networks, where evolving air--water interfaces strongly influence liquid invasion and gas displacement. Here, pore-resolved, image-based direct numerical simulations (DNS) are used to investigate spontaneous imbibition in a FIB--SEM-reconstructed cementitious microstructure, resolving air--water interface dynamics at nanometre-to-micrometre spatial scales and nanosecond-to-microsecond timescales. As these dynamics remain inaccessible to direct experimental observation at such scales, the simulations provide, to the best of our knowledge, the first direct view of transient imbibition within the capillary porosity of a realistic cementitious microstructure. The three-dimensional simulations reveal highly heterogeneous wetting-front propagation, continuous interface reconfiguration, and progressive air entrapment, showing that local dynamics depend on evolving interface curvature and capillary-pressure fields rather than on characteristic pore size alone. Significant air entrapment develops even within the capillary pores and under perfectly water-wetting conditions, progressively reducing the saturation rate, while the capillary pressure of trapped-air clusters depends strongly on local interface geometry rather than gas volume alone. Controlled two-dimensional analyses show that the balance between capillary, viscous, inertial, and gravitational effects is strongly scale-dependent. Comparison with the three-dimensional simulations highlights the importance of out-of-plane interface curvature and pore-network connectivity. The framework also resolves moisture conditions at the steel--concrete interface, illustrating its potential for corrosion-relevant pore-scale analysis.
item.dc:creator: Luka Malenica, Zhidong Zhang, Ueli Angst

item.title: Machine-Learned Interatomic Potential for the Mo-S-Al-O System
item.description: arXiv:2611.02403v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a machine-learned neuroevolution potential (NEP) for the Mo-S-Al-O system, targeting MoS$_2$ heteroepitaxy on c-plane sapphire, $\alpha$-Al$_2$O$_3$(0001). The potential is trained on 63,611 PBE+D3 structures distilled from about 1.1 million curated density-functional-theory (DFT) configurations, using an energy-difference loss function that directly targets interfacial and orientation-dependent energies. On held-out data, the energy and force errors are 29 meV/atom and 0.23 eV/$\mathring{A}$. Validated against DFT on a suite of physical properties, the NEP reproduces the lattice constants within 0.3 %, the elastic constants within 17 %, the phonon dispersions with mean deviations below 2.5%, and the surface energies within 1.3 %. At the MoS$_2$/sapphire interface, it reproduces the adhesion energy minimum within 0.8 %, the interfacial energy within 2.2 % and the most stable orientation of the monolayer. It preserves the DFT-predicted energetic ordering of edges, point defects (Spearman $\rho$ = 0.995) and mirror-twin boundaries ($\rho$ = 1.0), and reproduces tilt grain-boundary energies within 8 % ($\rho$ = 0.98) and stacking-fault energy barriers within 14 %. The resulting potential enables future studies of the atomic-scale mechanisms of defect formation in two-dimensional heteroepitaxy.
item.dc:creator: Emir Bilgili, Nicholas Taormina, Simon R. Phillpot, Youping Chen

item.title: Learning the Entropic Relaxation: Stable Coarse-Grid Emulation with Neural Discrete Equilibrium
item.description: arXiv:2611.02458v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The ability to emulate complicated and computationally-expensive physical systems in an efficient and stable manner is a popular motivation for scientific machine learning (SciML). Stable numerical solvers tend to be computationally expensive, as they attempt to resolve small (spatial and temporal) scales that receive and dissipate spectral energy. Learned coarse-grid forecasters remove the dissipative channel, allowing unresolved frequencies to re-emerge as grid-scale noise (aliasing). In this paper, we use the Neural Discrete Equilibrium (NeurDE) method to explore stable emulation at extremely coarse grids, demonstrating physically-principled control over entropy dynamics that reinforces the physical system's dissipative mechanism. Entropically-stabilized NeurDE produces stable long-time rollouts for thousands of forecasting steps on large Reynolds number turbulent flows ($\mathrm{Re}=100{,}000$) with very coarse grids (down to $\mathbb{R}^{16\times16}$). At these very coarse grid scales, entropically-stabilized NeurDE can be more stable than even our stabilized data-generation numerical method.
item.dc:creator: Jose Antonio Lara Benitez, Kareem Hegazy, Anastasis Kratsios, Ivan Dokmani\'{c}, Maarten V. de Hoop, Michael W. Mahoney

item.title: Computational performance versus numerical accuracy in the acoustic terms of weakly-compressible SPH
item.description: arXiv:2611.02994v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate computation of the acoustic terms in weakly-compressible SPH, including the equation of state, its inverse, and the evaluation of the local speed of sound, is essential to ensure energy conservation, robust solid boundary conditions, and correct open boundary behavior. In the classic Cole's equation of state, using values of the polytropic constant $\gamma \ne 1$ can lead to significant precision loss, particularly when computations are performed in single precision, as is common in GPU implementations. We extend here our previous results on the optimal choice of state variable by introducing a new higher-precision form for all three acoustic terms, denoted \texttt{explog}, and assess its numerical accuracy and computational performance across a variety of devices and test cases. We find that the new form evaluates the acoustic terms with a maximum ULP of~2 for arguments less than $0.125$, and has higher errors in less than 1\% of the arguments larger than the threshold. Combined with a rewritten expression of the pressure at solid boundary particles in the ``dummy'' model, it provides consistently more accurate results, maintaining deviations from the reference pressure profile to below 2\%, even in presence of a rough bottom terrain. Computationally, the new formulation is also faster than the naive one on GPU, and only marginally slower on CPU.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Bilotta, Alireza Zarei, Roberta Cristofaro, Alexis H\'erault, \'Elie Saikali, Morteza Derakhti

item.title: Mercury (Hg): a relativistic $N$-body simulation for Horndeski gravity
item.description: arXiv:2611.03637v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present Mercury, a relativistic $N$-body code for cosmological simulations in the $\alpha$-basis formulation of Horndeski gravity. Mercury extends a particle-mesh scheme by incorporating the dynamics of the additional scalar degree of freedom and the corresponding modified Einstein equations, expressed in terms of the time-dependent functions $\alpha_{\rm K}, \alpha_{\rm B}, \alpha_{\rm M}, \alpha_{\rm T}$ and the effective Planck mass $M_*^2$. This generalises our previous implementation of Horndeski subclass models, namely $k$-essence and kinetic gravity braiding (KGB), to the general linear Horndeski $\alpha$-basis. The code evolves the additional scalar degree of freedom and its effective stress--energy tensor alongside the nonlinear matter and metric fields, so that nonlinear structure formation sources the scalar-field evolution and feeds back on the gravitational potentials. Through its interface with hi_class, Mercury supports both phenomenological $\alpha$-function parametrisations and covariant Horndeski theories; we demonstrate the latter using nKGB, the Cubic Galileon, and Brans--Dicke models. We validate the implementation against hi_class in the linear regime and recover the expected nonlinear $k$-essence and KGB limits. For the luminal Horndeski models considered here, we show how a running effective Planck mass generates gravitational slip through the scalar anisotropic stress and modifies the friction terms governing the vector and tensor metric perturbations. The evolution of $M_*^2$ also modifies the normalisation and scale dependence of the effective dark-energy density contrast, leaving a corresponding imprint on its power spectrum. The present framework provides an intermediate step towards nonlinear Horndeski simulations, in which nonlinear scalar self-interactions and screening effects can be incorporated consistently within the same relativistic framework.
item.dc:creator: Ahmad Nouri-Zonoz, Farbod Hassani, Julian Adamek, Emilio Bellini, Martin Kunz

item.title: A Thin Sheet Volume Integral Equation Solver for Simulation of Bianisotropic Metasurfaces
item.description: arXiv:2604.21474v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A thin-sheet (TS) volume integral equation (VIE) formulation incorporating generalized sheet transition conditions (GSTCs) is presented for the simulation of three-dimensional (3D) bianisotropic metasurfaces. The metasurface is represented as an equivalent thin sheet, with its constitutive tensors derived from the GSTC susceptibility tensors. Invoking the thin-sheet approximation, the governing VIEs are reduced to surface integral equations (SIEs), in which tangential and normal flux density components are treated as distinct sets of unknowns and discretized using Rao-Wilton-Glisson and pulse basis functions, respectively. In contrast to conventional GSTC approaches based on conventional SIEs, which represent only tangential fields, the proposed framework rigorously enforces the bianisotropic GSTCs, including normal field interactions, while retaining the flux-based VIE character of the formulation. Numerical examples, including a comparison with an SIE-GSTC solver that neglects the normal susceptibility components, demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of the proposed TS-VIE-GSTC solver for polarization rotation on planar and curved sheets, perfect reflection, beam steering with spatially varying susceptibilities, multi-directional attenuation, and oblique phase-shift transformation.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Celis Sierra, Meruyert Khamitova, Ran Zhao, Sadeed Bin Sayed, Hakan Bagci

item.title: Annealing chains that communicate: low-energy cluster structures across engines with one configuration
item.description: arXiv:2302.02811v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The global minimum of a cluster decides which structure a simulation predicts. We present anneal, a global optimizer of communicating chains. Each chain draws its move by Thompson sampling from a Normal-Gamma posterior on quench depth. A stalled chain completes the orbits of a symmetric core. A chain retires on a Good-Turing estimate of its unseen mass, a rule with a Lean derivation. The chains share minima through an annealed-flow bank, and a ledger charges each force call to the chain that spent it. On 64 shared starts of LJ$_{38}$ and LJ$_{75}$ the hop matches the hit rate of GMIN, 64 of 64, at a lower median cost a paired test does not separate. On the Cambridge Morse table it reaches 145 of 244 targets and GMIN 131.
item.dc:creator: Rohit Goswami, Ruhila Goswami, Amrita Goswami, Moritz Sallermann, Sonaly Goswami, Debabrata Goswami

item.title: Kernel Ridge Regression for conformer ensembles made easy with Structured Orthogonal Random Features
item.description: arXiv:2505.21247v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A computationally efficient protocol for machine learning in chemical space using Boltzmann ensembles of conformers as input is proposed; the method is based on rewriting Kernel Ridge Regression expressions in terms of Structured Orthogonal Random Features, yielding physics-motivated trigonometric neural networks. To evaluate the method's utility for materials discovery, we test it on experimental datasets of two quantities related to battery electrolyte design, namely oxidation potentials in acetonitrile and hydration energies, using several geometry- and orbital-based molecular representations to demonstrate the method's flexibility. Despite only using computationally cheap force field calculations for conformer generation and generating orbital representations with GFN2-xTB calculations, we observe systematic decrease of prediction errors with increased training set size in all cases, with experimental accuracy reached after training on hundreds of molecules.
item.dc:creator: Konstantin Karandashev

item.title: Unified Learning of Interatomic Potentials and Electronic Hamiltonians, with Applications in 2D Materials
item.description: arXiv:2510.16605v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce UnIPH, an equivariant graph neural network designed to jointly predict both interatomic potentials and tight-binding (TB) Hamiltonians for an atomic structure. UnIPH is trained using density functional theory (DFT) calculations followed by Wannier projection to predict energies and forces as node-level targets and Wannier-projected TB Hamiltonians as edge-level targets. This enables physically consistent modeling of coupled mechanical-electronic responses with near-DFT-level accuracy. After separately training two UnIPH models on DFT data for bilayer graphene and monolayer MoS2, respectively, we find that these models capture key deformation-electronic effects: in twisted bilayer graphene, the trained UnIPH reveals how interlayer spacing, in-plane strain, and out-of-plane corrugation drive isolated flat-band formation, and further shows that modulating substrate interaction strength can generate flat bands even away from the magic angle (approximately 1.1 degrees). For monolayer MoS2, UnIPH accurately reproduces phonon dispersions and strain-dependent band-gap evolution, and further predicts how a non-uniform substrate creates localized strain pockets that spatially modulate the conduction- and valence-band edges.
item.dc:creator: Moon-ki Choi, Daniel Palmer, Shivam Sharma, Harley T. Johnson

item.title: Achieving angular-momentum conservation with physics-informed neural networks in computational relativistic spin hydrodynamics
item.description: arXiv:2512.17971v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a numerical solver for relativistic spin hydrodynamics and demonstrate that the total angular momentum, i.e., the sum of orbital and spin angular momentum, is accurately conserved throughout the fluid evolution by imposing the conservation law directly in the loss function as a training target. This enables controlled numerical studies of the mutual conversion between spin and orbital angular momentum, a central feature of relativistic spin hydrodynamics driven by the rotational viscous effect. We present two physical scenarios with a rotating fluid confined in a cylindrical container: one case in which initial orbital angular momentum is converted into spin angular momentum in analogy with the Barnett effect, and the opposite case in which initial spin angular momentum is converted into orbital angular momentum in analogy with the Einstein-de Haas effect. We investigate these conversion processes governed by the rotational viscous effect by analyzing the spacetime profiles of thermal vorticity and spin potential. Our PINNs-based framework provides the first numerical evidence for spin-orbit angular momentum conversion with fully nonlinear computational relativistic spin hydrodynamics.
item.dc:creator: Hidefumi Matsuda, Koichi Hattori, Koichi Murase

item.title: NeuralCrop: Combining physics and machine learning for improved crop modelling
item.description: arXiv:2512.20177v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Global gridded crop models (GGCMs) are crucial for projecting climate impacts on agricultural productivity and assessing associated risks to food security. However, state-of-the-art GGCMs are subject to substantial uncertainties arising from reduced representations of complex processes. Projected increases in the frequency and severity of climate extremes require more reliable agricultural yield simulations. Recent machine learning approaches trained on observational data provide alternatives to GGCMs, but remain under-constrained due to sparse observations and show poor out-of-distribution generalization. Here we introduce NeuralCrop, a differentiable hybrid GGCM that combines the strengths of an advanced process-based GGCM (LPJmL) with data-driven components. NeuralCrop is first trained to reproduce its underlying fully process-based version, before it is fine-tuned on observational flux data of physiological variables. Evaluation against held-out flux-tower observations from European wheat and US maize sites shows 32.6-45.2% reductions in mean normalized root-mean-square error for daily carbon and water fluxes. Although fine-tuned only on physiological variables, NeuralCrop improves temporal correlations with independent yield records across 71.4% of the cultivated area for European wheat and 84.0% for the US Corn Belt during 1981-2019. It performs highly competitively compared to GGCMI Phase~3 models. NeuralCrop reproduces yield anomalies more accurately across a range of soil-moisture conditions and especially for extreme drought conditions. For large-scale, long-term simulations, NeuralCrop runs nearly two orders of magnitude faster than the CPU-based LPJmL baseline model, mainly thanks to GPU acceleration. Our results highlight end-to-end hybrid crop modelling as a promising avenue for improving crop simulations and informing food security assessments under climate change.
item.dc:creator: Yunan Lin, Sebastian Bathiany, Maha Badri, Maximilian Gelbrecht, Philipp Hess, Brian Groenke, Jens Heinke, Christoph M\"uller, Niklas Boers

item.title: COACH: Toward the performance limit of traditional hybrid density functionals for molecular chemistry
item.description: arXiv:2603.23466v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) offers an exceptional balance between accuracy and efficiency, but practical density functional approximations face an unavoidable trade-off among simplicity, accuracy, and transferability. Here we present a systematic functional-development protocol that combines constraint enforcement, flexible functional forms, and modern optimization within a predefined application domain and functional class. Applying this strategy to the range-separated hybrid (RSH) meta-GGA framework, we obtain the carefully optimized and appropriately constrained hybrid (COACH) functional. Across broad molecular benchmarks, COACH improves both accuracy and transferability relative to leading RSH meta-GGAs, including \(\omega\)B97M-V, while retaining the computational practicality of its rung. These results suggest that COACH comes closer to the performance limit of traditional hybrid meta-GGA functionals for general molecular ground-state chemistry. Further substantial progress will likely require richer nonlocal or orbital-dependent information than is available from semilocal density ingredients combined with simple exact-exchange mixing.
item.dc:creator: Jiashu Liang, Martin Head-Gordon

item.title: All-electron Dynamical Bethe-Salpeter Equation for Extended Systems with Atom-centered Orbital Basis
item.description: arXiv:2606.08350v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Solving Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) for the two-particle Green's function is the most widely used approach for taking into account the particle-hole (exciton) interaction in electronic excitation in the context of the many-body theory based on Green's function. In BSE calculations, the static approximation to the screened Coulomb interaction kernel is commonly employed. However, when the excitonic character is significant as typically indicated by a large exciton binding energy, dynamical screening effects become non-negligible, rendering the static approximation questionable. Because of the large computational cost due to the dense Brillouin zone integration necessary for convergence, solving the dynamical BSE for extended systems remains a significant challenge, especially when combined with GW calculation for the calculation of quasi-particle energies. In this work, we formulate the plane-wave based effective dielectric function method [Zhang, et al., Phys. Rev. B 107, 235205 (2023)] for the dynamical BSE calculation using atom-centered orbitals as basis functions. We implement this approach in our recently developed all-electron numerical atom-centered orbital (NAO) implementation of BSE@GW [Zhou, et. al. J. Chem. Theory Comput. 21, 291 (2025)] for extended systems. We validate our all-electron NAO-based implementation of the dynamical BSE method, and we then discuss its realistic application to molecular crystal of naphthalene by performing the dynamical BSE@G0W0 calculation.
item.dc:creator: Ruiyi Zhou, Songrui Liu, Jianhang Xu, Yi Yao, Yosuke Kanai

item.title: Graph-Based Kirchhoff Modeling of Non-Ohmic Electron Transport in Self-Assembled Nanonecklace Networks
item.description: arXiv:2607.03698v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gold nanonecklace networks exhibit non-Ohmic current--voltage I-V characteristics with a sharp conduction threshold, making them promising for sensing and transistor-like devices. However, their conduction has been understood largely empirically, because experiments cannot see how conduction evolves inside the network. To address this, we develop a graph-based Kirchhoff modeling framework that resolves these internal processes, tracking the potential and current of every junction. Although every active element conducts linearly, the model reproduces the non-Ohmic response $I \propto (V-V_T)^\zeta$. It also captures the experimentally observed effects of junction properties, network density, and voids, which lends confidence to its predicted internal states. These states show that the non-Ohmic response emerges from voltage-driven percolation. Conduction is governed by how junctions are connected rather than by how many are active, with the current scaling approximately as \(N^{2.3}\) while the number of active junctions grows only linearly. Contrary to the expectation that junction heterogeneity strengthens the nonlinear response, homogeneous junctions in a well-connected network produce the most abrupt and reproducible turn-on. Thus, each structural parameter acts as a distinct control knob. The mean junction characteristics set the threshold, junction uniformity sets the switching sharpness, and network density and voids set the connectivity and current. These relationships provide design rules for tailoring nanonecklace networks to a desired conduction behavior through synthesis and fabrication.
item.dc:creator: Obed Issakah, Md Khirul Alam Titu, Srivathsan Badrinarayanan, Ravi F. Saraf, Janghoon Ock

item.title: Computational Fluid Dynamics and Discrete Dipole Approximation Applied to Predict Airborne Viruses Disinfection by Ultraviolet Irradiation
item.description: arXiv:2607.06746v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ultraviolet (UV) inactivation of airborne viruses involves coupled multiphysics and multiscale processes, yet UV scattering within virus-laden saliva droplets is commonly neglected. Here, for the first time we combine computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and the discrete dipole approximation (DDA) to investigate the influence of droplet-scale UV scattering on airborne virus inactivation. A benchmark CFD-DDA case study is developed and demonstrated that infected saliva droplets can exhibit highly non-uniform UV scattering under representative flow and irradiance conditions. This non-uniformity can substantially affect the predicted number of surviving viral copies, $N_s$ , indicating that UV scattering should be considered when modeling UV-based airborne disinfection systems. We systematically investigate the effect on $N_s$ by varying: the initially emitted saliva droplets diameter distribution, their number ($n(t = 0) = 10^3$ or $10^4$), volumetric airflow rate ($Q_v$ = 100, 150, or 200 $m^3/h$), droplet-wall interaction (stick vs escape), and coronavirus UV susceptibility constant (Z = 0.018 or 0.377 $m^2$/J). The simulations consider initially infected saliva droplets containing $7.4 \times 10^8$ RNA copies/mL, with a viral capsid diameter of $d_{cap}$ = 100 nm, at an air temperature of 21 {\deg}C and relative humidity of 65%. UV irradiation is represented by a 10 W cylindrical UV-lamp (34.3 mW/$cm^2$). The DDA results further enable development of an extended virus-inactivation model based on the classical Chick-Watson law that accounts for UV scattering in both spherical and nonspherical infected droplets. The results highlight the importance of resolving local UV-droplet interactions in airborne virus disinfection models and demonstrate the potential of the coupled CFD-DDA approach for improving the design and performance of UV-based airborne disinfection systems.
item.dc:creator: Talib Dbouk, Maxim Yurkin

item.title: Derivative Computation in PINNs: Automatic Differentiation, Finite Differences and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2608.11020v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We systematically investigate finite-difference (FD) derivative computation in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) as an alternative to automatic differentiation (AD). On three benchmark PDEs we show that, with a properly calibrated step size, FD matches AD in accuracy on every problem while running faster across the full tested batch-size range and using substantially less GPU memory, and that a stochastic variant we propose outperforms AD on a stationary problem. We further show that for neural architectures with inter-sample dependencies (e.g. BatchNorm, self-attention) the standard PyTorch autograd idiom is silently incorrect; the correct per-sample alternative is computationally infeasible at PINN-relevant batch sizes, while FD provides a forward-only approximation that is empirically an order of magnitude closer to the true per-sample derivative.
item.dc:creator: Maciej J. Mikulski, Tadeusz Uhl

item.title: Characteristic Mapping Method for Vlasov-Poisson with BGK-collisions
item.description: arXiv:2609.16328v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This work presents the first steps for simulating kinetic plasmas with collisions using the characteristic mapping method (CMM). The CMM is a semi-Lagrangian method that uses the group structure of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms to efficiently represent the flow-maps of transport problems. Individual submaps can be composed to follow the flow backward in time to its initial foot point, numerically establishing the back-to-label symmetry. The novelty of the presented work is the handling of the source term by storing the Duhamel integrals of each time sub-interval, allowing efficient temporal-integration. Furthermore, we use the Lagrangian structure to avoid implicit time-stepping in the hydrodynamic regime, which is known to be stiff. We benchmark our method on the Boltzmann-BGK and Vlasov-Poisson-BGK equations and consider different test cases, the Sod shock tube problem and nonlinear Landau damping for different Knudsen numbers. We show third-order spatial and temporal convergence and illustrate the fine-scale zoom property of CMM for the bump-on-tail instability.
item.dc:creator: Xi-Yuan Yin, Philipp Krah, Zetao Lin, Jean-Christophe Nave, Kai Schneider

item.title: Residual correction for accelerating dual-time-stepping lattice Boltzmann methods
item.description: arXiv:2609.39474v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For lattice Boltzmann simulations of unsteady flows at low Reynolds numbers, dual-time stepping decouples the physical time step from lattice streaming, yet conserved-moment iteration errors decay slowly at large steps. We develop a residual correction method based on the conserved-moment structure of the collision operator. With fixed step histories and both relaxation rates equal to unity, post-collision populations depend on incoming populations only through reconstructed conserved moments, so one collision eliminates local perturbations with zero conserved moments. Periodic rest-state linearization shows that, at large physical steps, the contraction factor of the uniform conserved mode approaches unity, while its moment residual scales inversely with the step relative to macroscopic error. On periodic domains, combining this scaling with linearized acoustic propagation and viscous diffusion yields a macroscopic auxiliary system driven by the conserved-moment residual and solved in Fourier space for low-wavenumber errors. For solid walls, reference-state linearization of the complete sweep, including executed bounce-back updates, yields a sparse kinetic correction. Both auxiliary systems compute increments from the full nonlinear residual, and we prove fixed-point equivalence with the original discrete system, preserving unsteady and nonlinear convective effects. Refining the time step on fixed grids verifies second-order temporal self-convergence of slowly varying periodic velocity fields in two and three dimensions. Under fixed physical steps and tolerances, mean inner sweeps per step drop from hundreds in three-dimensional periodic flow and thousands in a two-dimensional cavity to a few.
item.dc:creator: Yanhui Ding, Yaolong Yu, Yuan Yu, Hao Zhang

item.title: Learning qBIC Resonances across Metasurface Families in Dielectric Fourier Space
item.description: arXiv:2610.11500v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BIC) metasurfaces are typically described by geometry-specific parameters, hindering cross-geometry comparison, while ultranarrow quasi-BIC (qBIC) features are easily diluted in full-spectrum learning. Here, we map 2,015 samples from seven dielectric metasurface families onto a shared reciprocal-lattice grid. Two fixed low-order Fourier descriptors capture within-branch resonance shifts, with mean $R^2$ values of 0.871-0.999. Field-level analysis of two representative branches shows that these shifts are consistent with the Maxwell-Fourier perturbation picture. A five-channel Fourier-space backbone models the broadband spectrum. A local resonance expert uses complex Fourier coefficients to parameterize the qBIC resonance through a differentiable Fano layer. The expert reduces resonance-position mean absolute error (MAE) from 3.2 to 0.95 nm and reduces the minimum-transmission MAE by a factor of 14 on a geometry-blocked test set. The same coordinate supports spectrum-to-structure reconstruction.
item.dc:creator: Shuangteng Lei, Li Yu, Tianxin Li, Wei Lu
